records.title: Show HN: Isometric SF – A pixel-art map of the SF Bay Area
records.author: juscha1
records.storyText:
Technical Write-up: https://www.justinchavez.com/blog/isometric-sf-how/

Hi HN! Showcasing this fun project. I took 1300 square miles of the SF Bay Area from Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and transformed them into a cohesive pixel map. It's really fun to explore and stumble upon various famous landmarks like Apple Park, Palace of Fine Arts, or UC Berkeley.

The technicals involve using Nano Banana 2 to train a Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 LoRA which is used to prototype the style and generation methods. For final map I used Qwen to train a Klein 4B LoRA which reproduced the style at 1/4 of the cost. More details in the blog post.

Let me know what you think! I really enjoyed this process of fine-tuning smaller open source models.

If I did the map with Nano Banana 2 it would have cost around 7k USD!

Credit for the idea goes to Isometric NYC.

Hey HN readers!

I'm snipedbywifi (https://gitlab.com/snipedbywifi), and i've been working on terminactory. Please try it out if you'd like to play a cozy factory game while waiting for long agent tasks to finish!

The game is a factory game (overused niche, i know xD), but runs in your terminal. Reason i built it? glad you asked: So basically, it started off with me wanting a terminal-native factory game. Me and the modern 5.5 claude models made a base for the game that I liked, and then i went ham adding features / fixing some minor flaws (like adding claude code hooks so you recieve "telegrams" [the agent's responses], so you can review progress directly in-game). (yes, I had heavy AI assistance, disclaimer!!!)

Right now, the game has basic factory features you'd expect from a game like this (build stuff, delete stuff, measure how much you're earning, basic selection tools), along with a few more.. "unexpected" features. This includes a fake in-game browser that has a wiki, fake forums, some fun bits of lore, some more lore, a LOT more lore, and a research graph that shows how many items or how much RP (research points) you'd need to unlock something, and some more QOL features.

If anyone actually has this issue / want of a terminal-based game that runs alongside your agents so you don't doomscroll, do you have any suggestions, or additional ideas I could add?

It's hosted on GitLab, soo, that's one additional thing i'd like to mention

Thanks for reading!! snipedbywifi

(p.s. first HN post lol) (p.s. p.s. there's a lot of hidden lore in the game, so.. lore-divers? you might like it?)

records.title: Show HN: I have trained a model to predict my blood sugar
records.author: 0xdeadf1sh
records.storyText:
I have trained a custom 31,253 parameter encoder-only transformer on a pregenerated synthetic CGM dataset and fitted it to my own personal data using LoRA. It is competitive among other published models. I used 115 days of CGM data, of which 80 was used for training the adapter and 35 for testing. The model began with a pretraining stage where it consumed ~19,200 CGM-years worth of synthetic data, consisting of 1 million simulated type 1 diabetics at 7 days each. The simulator is designed to aid in counterfactual reasoning, but I don't yet have a benchmark to test these capabilities downstream. Simply using these models on my phone gives me the impression that they do indeed react appropriately when forced to consider future insulin & carbs.

In addition to time series input, two additional inputs are provided: insulin (U) and carbs (G, GI) as action curves where U = units of insulin, G = carbs in grams, GI = glycemic index. U is exact, while (G, GI) is my best estimate.

The model is trained to output BG in Kovatchev risk-space using {DILATE,MSE} and pinball loss combined with learned Kendall-Gal weights. The figures above show models trained using DILATE. It can predict 2 hours into the future, infill missing traces, and do backcasts (predictions into the past).

The model is also trained to predict time-of-day given past blood sugar, in contrast to other models that consume time-of-day as input feature. This capability emerges in >=48h context windows (i.e. 48 hours of past CGM trace). Natively the model has a variable context window size of 3.5 - 7.0 days.

The model is still worse than me when it comes to predicting hypoglycemia in the next ~30 minutes.

Hi everyone! I've created a web app where one can explore topics on mindmap-like canvas with text, images, videos, interactive nodes. One can also add sources, choose different models for different roles and many more.

I'm in my fifth year of psychiatry residency and have adhd and always hated learning from textbooks or lately through chat interface, where I easily loose information from sight, can't branch out and generally feel constrained. records.title: Show HN: Yet another agent manager (but we needed it)
records.author: imakris
records.storyText:
Hello HN,

I am Ioannis and I would like to introduce Logonomic, a desktop application we made to help us work with LLM CLIs (e.g. codex, claude, opencode etc) in a more organized way. It runs the CLIs already installed, with their existing accounts and configuration and organizes sessions by repository. It is available for Windows and Linux, with a preview for macOS. There is also a mobile companion app, to work remotely (Android and soon iOS too).

We built it originally to assist us in our own work, to address the common case of multiple agents running concurrently in many repositories. It was hard to keep track of what each one is doing and which one needs attention or requires action.

There are many tools by now broadly that broadly target the same problem. This one is a native C++/Qt application with our own terminal emulator. Some of its features:

- An 'overview' mode that shows all running sessions, optionally grouped by repository, each with its status, title and summary that the agents update regularly.

- Agents add a trailer to their commits, enabling to re-open the conversations that produced them.

- Terminals run in their own processes and survive UI crashes.

- A plot that shows line counts over time, by directory or language, where clicking on a sample brings up the corresponding commit in the git log.

- A treemap that shows how the repo's files are organized, with a diff mode that colours changed files, whose diff opens with a double click.

- Token usage and remaining account quotas shown where available, with usage broken down by day and repository.

- Sessions can exchange messages (1:1 or broadcast), may hand tasks to each other or continue other session's work.

The supported CLIs are Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, Grok Build, Kimi Code and Qwen Code.

The free edition has no time limit and runs up to four terminals. The paid editions have perpetual one-time licences from €150 for 2 seats and include 12 months of feature updates, no terminal limit, GitHub/GitLab CI integrations, as well as an Android companion app (iOS will follow).

The application itself is proprietary. Many of its core components are open source, among them the terminal emulator and the plotting library: https://github.com/Varinomics

This is the first public release, so there will be rough edges, and we would like to hear about them.

records.title: Show HN: String#to_proc` to Help Traversing JSON
records.author: samleb34
records.storyText:
I've resuscitated a project I was working on years ago.

I was tired of having nested `flat_map` making my code basically unreadable just to fetch a simple value. The idea is to make simple & readable the traversing of deeply nested structures like JSON responses, while staying in Ruby & keeping its flexibility. Here it goes:

    graphql_response.then(&'[data][repository][issues][edges]*([node][title])')
    # => ["Support negative indexes", "Document aggregates"]

    github_prs_response.then(&'*[draft].any?')
    # => true
It's different from jq or JSONPath in that: - it's a Ruby block so you can use it with `map`, `find`, etc. - you can call Ruby method from it - it doesn't automatically flatten arrays, you decide - it raises on `nil` by default (unless you use `&`, i.e. `[customer][address]&[city]`)

Obviously, it has drawbacks: - it's yet another syntax to learn - it monkey-patches `String` which might be a blocker for some

I'm really looking for feedback here, what do you think? Is it worth releasing a gem with this value proposition?

records.author: ragdollk
records.storyText:
Hi All,

I'm Kanton, one of the makers of bwat. Our team at Qoral built bwat because we wanted an easy way to take what we were talking about in meetings and get that work to our agent sessions with full context and quickly start them working.

So we created a Zoom app that is a board that generates cards based off the transcripts of the meeting. Transcription happens with Deepgram and has user attribution, voice isolation, and all the benefits of a native Zoom app.

The cards are todos (the work), unanswered questions, open risks, and decisions that have been made. They change over the course of the meeting, getting closed or updated based off the conversation. JEV helps to make these dynamic changes. Users can assign work to themselves by just saying so, instantaneously.

We worked on the setup and install process to try and make it as straight forward as possible. Setting up a Zoom app isn't able to be fully automated. The source code is available. Bring your own keys.

We'd most like to hear if people find this intuitive and can see the value in the meetings. It's certainly helped us with alignment and quick actions in our workflow.

Thanks!

records.storyText:
SrcWranglr my open-source, Rust-powered C/C++ source-code exploration and security analysis toolkit. I had originally developed this in Python as a prototype for a couple years… That’s until you Rustaceans got in my damn year…

If you ever used SourceTrail or Understand, this is my idea of how it should have been done. It helps visualize complex codebases C/C++ it combines interactive call graphs, cross-references, semantic code search, reachability analysis, and inter-procedural value tracing.

Security-focused features include vulnerability discovery, attack-surface analysis, automated fuzz harness generation, and integration with external static analyzers. My favorite feature is the ability to generate semgrep rules for the specific code base.

Powered by tree-sitter, SrcWranglr can analyze codebases without requiring a successful build or compilation database.

Using this tool and my AAVR (Agentic Augmented Vuln Research) methodology I found several vulnerabilities in projects I won’t name as I just disclose to maintainers, in just a couple of hours.

https://github.com/jdefrancesco/SrcWranglr

records.title: Show HN: FieldRook – a local-first Windows troubleshooting workstation
records.author: nullfeather
records.storyText:
Please have a look at my opensource project FieldRook, here is a short description over it.

I am working as a Onsite Technichan in Sweden and i got tired of trying to puzzle togheter different windows-logs and throubleshooting steps to get forward in our tickets, and the logging started to get a real nightmare. Specially to prove for the users why it actually solved the problem and not just giving them a random "Well, it said so in the guide i read"-Type of answer.

So I started building a Windowsapp that actually collects diagnostics, traceable observartions, hypothesis and verificiations. AI is a chooseble option and not something that gets direct access to run commands and such.

This is a first hand version, it's currently unsigned and needs a much larger field-testing on windowsmachines. I have a hard time testing it inside our work-domain thanks to all of our security policys and such, so have mostly been running it on my local PC at home. If someone would like to have a go at it, please check out the GitHub-repo and download it and give me some feedback on what you liked and not. What worked and not.

If other people that work in IT-support actually tried it, do you think it would actually help out in a day-to-day basis? What would you change in it, what is missing and how would you concider the securitymodel at the moment?

Thanks in advance!

records.title: Show HN: Host a site, content, or stream from a browser tab, served over WebRTC
records.author: bromney
records.storyText:
Site URL: https://fmrl.live

Repository URL: https://gitlab.com/croatoa/fmrl

This project allows you to host a website, content, and streaming from an open browser window. It gets served over WebRTC connections (or a Cloudfare turn server if that's not available).

This is just a start. Any suggestions or feedback to improve usability, feature requests, etc is super welcome.

This is a project I've had in mind for a while. I wanted to participate in building for a decentralized web, so I thought it would be cool if people could run a social network kind of page from their own machine, and allow them to diffuse content over a peer to peer net, independent of the typical social media giants.

While this iteration is not quite that, it's a start.

While the UI probably makes this super obvious, this is the first time I've used AI in coding (LLM, Claude Code). It really is some impressive machinery.

The goal isn't privacy, but rather autonomy, more or less. I know there are real limitations (like a host user closing their browser) but I feel like the idea is at least slightly novel (probably because its a mediocre idea lol).. but it'll be interesting to see how it evolves.

If you made it this far, thanks for the read. Hope you have a pleasant day.

records.title: Show HN: Port of Context – Token efficient MCP context layer
records.author: pmkelly4444
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm working on a context layer built on OSS and open standards that lets agents search your company knowledge and use MCP tools all through a single gateway with code mode. Building this because we believe context can and should be portable across harnesses.

The metric we are solving for here is "cost to resolution". Given any question or a task, how quickly and cheaply can we put an agent on the correct path. Tech behind that:

1. Context map: software to create and maintain a context map of people, teams, systems, relationships, etc. It's built on OKF, import/export from this open standard.

2. Code mode: agents explore the map with a token efficient context eng. method (open source runtime, find portofcontext/pctx on GitHub)

3. Indexing: Hybrid keyword and semantic search on any unstructured text, with code mode on top (we will open source this part soon, although it's nothing special, the interesting part is placing content in the map and putting code mode on it)

Some proof that it works:

1. Goose + code mode: https://aaif.io/blog/how-port-of-context-eliminated-producti...

2. tau-bench: https://portofcontext.com/blog/context-layer-platform-benchm... With Port of Context

To try it, paste this into your coding agent: Set up pctx.ai/onboard.md

It will help you create an account, scan your active MCP connections, and help configure the gateway.

Hope you find this useful and feel free to reach out: patrick@portofcontext.com
